pages.h: It all starts with the Sun
p: Every bit of weather starts with the Sun. The Sun warms the ground. The ground warms the air. Warm air is light, so it floats up. Cool air slides in to take its place. That is how wind begins. No Sun, no weather.
pages.cap: Heat from the Sun warms the ground, and the ground warms the air.

pages.h: Wind is air on the move
p: You cannot see air. But you can feel it when it moves. Moving air is called wind. A soft wind can lift a kite. A strong wind can push a sailboat. The fastest wind ever measured at a weather station blew at 408 kilometres an hour, on an island in Australia.
pages.cap: Moving air can lift a kite, a bird, or a plane.
pages.fact: Did you know? Wind has no colour, but you can see what it does to leaves, flags and hair.

pages.h: A cloud is made of tiny drops
p: A cloud looks soft and dry. It is not. A cloud is billions of tiny water drops floating in the air. Each drop is far smaller than a grain of sand. They are so light that the air holds them up. Walk through fog and you are inside a cloud.
pages.cap: Tiny drops gather high in the sky and make a cloud.

pages.q: What is a cloud made of?
pages.why: A cloud is billions of tiny water drops floating in the air.

p: After rain there is a puddle. The Sun comes out. Later the puddle is gone. Where did it go? The Sun warmed the water. It turned into a gas called water vapour. You cannot see it. It floated up into the sky to make new clouds.
pages.cap: Warm water turns into a gas and floats up into the air.

p: High in a cloud, tiny drops bump into each other. They join and grow. When a drop gets heavy, the air cannot hold it. It falls. That is rain. A raindrop is not shaped like a tear. It is round, like a tiny hamburger bun.
pages.cap: Drops join together until they are heavy enough to fall.
pages.fact: Did you know? A big raindrop falls at about 30 kilometres an hour.

pages.h: The water in your cup is older than the dinosaurs
p: Water goes up as vapour, comes down as rain, and goes up again. Round and round, for billions of years. The rain today may once have been sipped by a dinosaur.

When a cloud is very cold, water vapour freezes straight into tiny ice crystals. They grow into snowflakes. Almost every snowflake has six sides. Look closely at one on your sleeve. No two are exactly the same. Snow is not frozen rain. Frozen raindrops are called sleet.
pages.cap: Frozen water locks into a pattern with six sides.
pages.fact: Did you know? Some parts of Canada get more than 4 metres of snow in one winter.

p: Lightning is a giant spark in a storm cloud. It is hotter than the surface of the Sun. It heats the air so fast that the air bangs. That bang is thunder. You see the flash first, because light moves faster than sound. Count the seconds between them.
pages.cap: Count: every 3 seconds between flash and boom means the storm is 1 kilometre away.
pages.fact: Did you know? Lightning can be five times hotter than the surface of the Sun.

p: Stand with the Sun behind you. Rain falls in front of you. Look! A rainbow. Sunlight goes into each raindrop and splits into seven colours. Red is on the outside. Purple is on the inside. You can never reach the end of a rainbow. It moves when you move.
pages.cap: Sun behind you, rain in front of you, rainbow in the middle.

pages.q: Why do you see lightning before you hear thunder?
pages.why: Light races to your eyes almost at once. Sound takes about 3 seconds to travel 1 kilometre.

p: A tornado is wind that spins. It drops out of a storm cloud like a twisting finger. Inside, the wind can blow faster than 300 kilometres an hour. It can lift a car. Canada gets more than 60 tornadoes a year. If one comes, go to the basement.
pages.cap: A tornado is a spinning tube of wind that touches the ground.

p: A hurricane is a storm as big as a country. It grows over warm ocean water. It spins slowly, like a giant pinwheel. In the very middle is a calm, quiet hole called the eye. In 2022, a hurricane called Fiona hit Nova Scotia and knocked down thousands of trees.
pages.cap: From space, a hurricane looks like a huge white spiral.

p: Hail is ice that falls in summer! Inside a tall storm cloud, wind throws a drop up and down. Each trip up adds a new coat of ice. At last it is too heavy and drops. The biggest hailstone found in Canada was about 12 centimetres across. That is bigger than a tennis ball.
pages.cap: Hailstones grow inside the same tall clouds that make thunder.

p: Measure how much rain falls at your home.
steps: Find a jar or cup with straight sides.
Put it outside in an open spot before it rains.
After the rain, measure the water with a ruler in millimetres.
Write the number down. Try again on the next rainy day.
pages.cap: Make a chart of your rain, one bar for each day.
pages.safe: Do not go out during a thunderstorm.

pages.h: Fog is a cloud on the ground
p: Sometimes a cloud forms right down where you are. We call it fog. It happens when the air near the ground gets cool and damp. Fog can hide a whole street. Cars turn on their lights. Then the Sun warms the air and the fog turns back into vapour.
pages.cap: Fog can hide the tops of tall buildings.

p: The Earth is tilted a little, like a leaning top. It goes around the Sun once a year. When your part of the Earth leans toward the Sun, the days are long and hot. That is summer. When it leans away, the days are short and cold. That is winter.
pages.cap: The tilt of the Earth gives us summer and winter.

p: Watch one tree for a whole year. In spring, buds open and new leaves unfold. In summer, the tree is full and green. In autumn, the leaves turn red and gold and drop. In winter, the branches are bare and wait for spring.
pages.cap: The same tree in spring, summer, autumn and winter.

pages.q: When is it summer where you live?
opts: When your part of Earth leans toward the Sun
When Earth is closest to the Moon
pages.why: The tilt of the Earth makes seasons. Leaning toward the Sun means long, warm days.

p: A thermometer tells how hot the air is. On a nice summer day it says about 25 degrees Celsius. The hottest day ever in Canada was 49.6 degrees, in Lytton, British Columbia, in 2021. The coldest was minus 63 degrees, in Snag, Yukon, in 1947. Brr!
pages.cap: A thermometer measures how hot or cold the air is.

p: How do people know if it will rain tomorrow? Weather watchers send up balloons twice a day. Satellites take pictures of clouds from space. Then big computers crunch all the numbers. They make a guess called a forecast. It is often right. But not always!
pages.cap: Computers crunch millions of numbers to guess tomorrow's weather.

p: Other planets have weather too. Mars has dust storms that can cover the whole planet. Jupiter has a storm called the Great Red Spot. It is wider than the Earth. It has been spinning for more than 150 years. No umbrella could help you there.
pages.cap: The Great Red Spot on Jupiter is a storm bigger than our whole planet.

pages.h: A cloud can weigh as much as 100 elephants
p: A big, puffy summer cloud holds about 500,000 kilograms of water. But the drops are so tiny and spread out that the air can hold them all up.
Split sunlight into colours.
steps: Fill a clear glass with water right to the top.
Put it on a sunny windowsill, with the edge hanging over a little.
Lay a sheet of white paper on the floor below it.
Look for a tiny rainbow on the paper. Move the glass to find it.
pages.cap: The water bends the light and splits it into colours.
pages.safe: Never look straight at the Sun.
